> warning message;
> In vnames(FLAT,"ov.x", warn=TRUE)
> lavaan warning; model syntax contains variance/covariance/intercept
> formulas involving (an) exogenous variable(s)

Somewhere in your model syntax, you have specified either a variance, a
covariance or an intercept involving an exogenous (independent)
variable. By default, there is no reason to do so, because lavaan uses
the fixed.x=TRUE argument, implying that the exogenous variables are not
part of the model.

Simply removing these formulas from your syntax should work. To find out
which variables are exogenous, try:

lavNames( lavaanify(myModel), type="ov.x" )

The alternative is to use fixed.x=FALSE, which is mostly harmless, as
long as all your exogenous variables are continuous.

Yves.

Moreover, using the 'delta' parameterization, we can allow for free 'scaling' parameters for the different time points (the first one is fixed to 1). For my own reference, this is the full syntax (using growth() in 0.5-13) for a simple growth model using artificial data:

example(growth)

Databin <- Demo.growth
Databin[,c("t1","t2","t3","t4")] <- lapply(Databin[,c("t1","t2","t3","t4")],
                                           cut, 2, labels=FALSE)

myModel <- '
   # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
   i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
   s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4

   # fix mean of intercept factor
   i ~ 0*1

   # equal thresholds
   t1 | a*t1
   t2 | a*t1
   t3 | a*t1
   t4 | a*t1

   # scales
   t1 ~*~ 1*t1
   t2 ~*~ NA*t2
   t3 ~*~ NA*t3
   t4 ~*~ NA*t4
'
fit <- growth(myModel, data=Databin, ordered=c("t1","t2","t3","t4"))
summary(fit)

This will produce identical results compared to the 'default' behaviour of Mplus.

Yves.

> > As with most statistical null-hypothesis tests, the null hypothesis here is that there is no discrepancy whatsoever between the observed sample moments (covariance matrix and mean vector) and those implied by the model, or by implication, that there is no discrepancy between the tested model and the population model that generated the data.  Unless you are testing a saturated model, there will always be some discrepancy, and the p value is the right-tail probability of observing a discrepancy at least as extreme as that between your model and data, given that the null is true.  So larger p-values may indicate that your model fits well (see counter-arguments in http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//0033-295X.107.2.358), and very small ones may indicate poor fit.
> >
> > However, in social sciences we are never likely to have the correct model (i.e., one that includes all variables that account for a given behavioral phenomenon); rather, we deal with useful approximations.  With large sample sizes (as are typically required for stable estimation in SEM), the chi-squared test is over-powered to detect even trivial discrepancies as statistically significant.  Alternative indices of fit (e.g., RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, and TLI) are ways of assessing whether the observed discrepancy is of any practical significance, similar to including a measure of effect size in a t-test or ANOVA. Hi all,

I am not sure whether this a question specifically about lavaan or more generally about SEM:

I am interested in comparing an unconstrained model (model 1) to one in which regression coefficients are constrained to be equal (model 2).

model1<- '
I =~ I1 + I2 + I3
U =~ U1 + U2 + U3
S =~ S1 + S2 + S3
F =~ F1 + F2 + F3
F ~ I + U + S
'
fit1 <- sem (model1, data=data, missing="ml")

model2 <-'
I =~ I1 + I2 + I3
U =~ U1 + U2 + U3
S =~ S1 + S2 + S3
F =~ F1 + F2 + F3
F ~ d1*I + d1*U + d1*S
'
fit2 <- sem (model2, data=data, missing="ml")

I have had success at making the comparison but I have noticed what I think is a strange pattern in the regression coefficients. In model1 regression coefficients were:

F ~ I   est = .11   se = .14   p = .43   std.lv <http://std.lv> = .14
F ~ U  est = .04  se = .06   p = .51   std.lv <http://std.lv> = .16
F ~ S  est = .05  se = .07   p = .42   std.lv <http://std.lv> = .10

In model 2 regression coefficients were:

F ~ I    est = .06   se = .02   p = .002   std.lv <http://std.lv> = .07
F ~ U   est = .06   se = .02   p = .002   std.lv <http://std.lv> = .22
F ~ S  est = .06   se = .02    p = .002   std.lv <http://std.lv> = .11

I see that the unstandardized regression coefficient is roughly the same from model 1 to model 2 but the standard error has decreased in model 2 (also resulting in a drop in p). My question is: what has caused this drop in standard error in model 2?

I apologize if this question is not appropriate for the lavaan group. If so, a point towards more appropriate resources would be very appreciated.

Thanks in advance,
Sarah

messages.body_plain:
> I see that the unstandardized regression coefficient is roughly the same
> from model 1 to model 2 but the standard error has decreased in model 2
> (also resulting in a drop in p). My question is: what has caused this
> drop in standard error in model 2?

More information.

Try

zapsmall( diag(lavaan:::computeExpectedInformation(fit1@Model,
samplestats=fit1@SampleStats)) )

and

zapsmall( diag(lavaan:::computeExpectedInformation(fit2@Model,
samplestats=fit2@SampleStats)) )

to get a rough idea of the 'information' per parameter (ignoring all
off-diagonal elements)

Then, compare to

zapsmall( diag(vcov(fit1)) )

and

zapsmall( diag(vcov(fit2)) )

The 'information' contained in the three separate regression
coefficients is 'added up'. So you got about 3x more information. The
variance-covariance matrix of the parameters is the inverse of the
information matrix, and the standard errors are its square-root diagonal
elements. More information, smaller standard errors.

Hope this helps,

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Corrected BIC
messages.body_plain:
> My question is, whether these two LGC models (Six occasions vs five occasions) be compared and selection of model with lower CBIC can be made?
>

For the 2 CBICs to be comparable, they need to be fit to the same data.  I have no idea why a 5-occasion vs 6-occasion LGC would be competing models -- the 6-occasion model is potentially just an extrapolation of the 5-occasion model to include a 6th occasion using the same growth parameters.  If you want to compare the CBICs from these two models you would have to include the data from the 6th occasion in the 5-occasion model.  You could simply saturate the 6th occasion measurements by allowing them to freely correlate with the residuals of the measurements on the first 5 occasions -- as if the 6th occasion measurements were auxiliary variables in a FIML estimation of the 5-occasion model.  Then both models would be fit to the same data, but the 6th occasion measurements would not add any degrees of freedom to the 5-occasion model, nor should they unduly influence the growth parameters fit to the 5 occasions.

Terry
